title: What ihram forbids
hook: no perfume, no cutting hair, no hunting, no quarrelling

segments.voice: Yesterday, ihram, the two white cloths, and your line: all dressed alike. Whose clothes did you manage to look past? Day one thousand one hundred twenty-three.

A pilgrim is standing at Arafah with the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ when his mount throws him. He falls, and he dies there, still in his two white cloths. The report is in Sahih al-Bukhari. The people around him turn to the Prophet: what now? His instructions are short. Wash him with water and lote leaves. Shroud him in his two cloths. Don't put perfume on him. Don't cover his head. Then the reason: he'll be raised on the Day of Resurrection still calling out the pilgrim's cry. Even death, in this story, doesn't take him out of ihram. Today, what that state holds a person back from.
screen: `A PILGRIM FALLS AT ARAFAH.` → `NO PERFUME. HEAD UNCOVERED.` → `RAISED STILL A PILGRIM.`

segments.voice: First, the body. Once a pilgrim is in ihram, some ordinary things stop. No perfume, on the skin or the cloth. No cutting hair, and the Qur'an tells pilgrims not to shave their heads until the offering has reached its place, so the haircut becomes part of the ending, not the middle. Scholars add nails to the same list. Second, the creatures. The Qur'an says plainly that wild game is not to be killed while on the pilgrimage, in surah five. A person who might hunt at home lets the animals of the sanctuary be. Third, the tongue, and this one surprises people. In surah two, Pickthall's translation reads: "there is (to be) no lewdness nor abuse nor angry conversation on the pilgrimage." Not just no fighting. No angry conversation. A crowd, the heat, the lines, the lost luggage, someone's elbow in the ribs, and the instruction is: don't argue. Of everything on the list, that one asks the most patience. Fourth, what the rules are for. Each one is something small and ordinary, a scent, a trim, a sharp word. None of them is wrong at home. In ihram, they're set down for a while. The two cloths from yesterday are what people see. The restraint is what they don't see, and it goes all the way down, past the skin. That's why the man who fell at Arafah was left unperfumed and bareheaded. The rules weren't a costume he could take off. They were the state he was in, and he stayed in it.
screen: `NO PERFUME, NO HAIRCUT.` · `LET THE WILD GAME BE.` · `NO ANGRY CONVERSATION.` · `THE RESTRAINT GOES ALL THE WAY DOWN.`

segments.voice: The practice: give up one habit for a day. Pick something small and ordinary, not something bad. Your usual scent. Checking the score. Having the last word in a disagreement. Settle, and breathe, and choose it now. Then picture the moment later today when the habit will reach for you, and picture letting it pass. If you pray, you can ask for help keeping it, in your own words or with a verse you know. If you don't, just hold the picture and breathe. The bell holds the time.
What ihram forbids. Perfume, cutting hair, hunting, and quarreling, set down while the pilgrim is in the sacred state. Today's word.
Your line: restraint is the dress. Today, keep the habit you chose set down until evening, and notice each time it reaches for you. Day one thousand one hundred twenty-three.

howItsDone: Pilgrims in ihram avoid perfume, cutting hair and nails, hunting, marital relations and quarreling until the rites release them; the details and the remedy for a slip are set out in each school of Islamic law.

fork.setup: a pilgrim in ihram falls from his mount at Arafah and dies. the people ask the Prophet how to prepare him. what does he say?
options: perfume him and shroud him in new cloth.
wash him, shroud him in his two cloths, no perfume, head uncovered.
send him home to be buried in his own clothes.
fork.reveal: he is left in the state of ihram, and the Prophet says he will be raised on the Day of Resurrection still calling the pilgrim's cry.

trapdoor: what you thought: a list of rules about clothes.
what it means: a state of restraint, body, creatures and tongue, that the cloth only shows.
what a scholar hears: 2:197 puts angry conversation beside lewdness, and Bukhari's fallen pilgrim stays in ihram even in death.

sources.quoted: there is (to be) no lewdness nor abuse nor angry conversation on the pilgrimage.

notes: Bukhari 1265 (Ibn Abbas: the man thrown by his mount at Arafah; wash with water and lote leaves, shroud in his two garments, no perfume, head uncovered, raised saying talbiyah): confirm number (parallels at 1266–1268, 1849–1851). The hook paraphrases 'raised saying talbiyah' as 'calling out the pilgrim's cry' to leave tomorrow's word for tomorrow.
Pickthall 2:197 quoted from memory, including the parentheses: confirm exact wording.
2:196 (do not shave your heads until the offering reaches its destination): paraphrased; confirm the reading is fair.
'Scholars add nails to the same list': general statement of fiqh; confirm.
howItsDone mentions marital relations (2:197 'rafath') and expiation in the schools; check wording.
